section_summary: This section documents U.S. diplomatic and Treasury inquiries into narcotics smuggling through Kobe, Osaka, Yokohama, Shanghai, and trans-Pacific shipping, including detailed allegations against Max Schwartz and his associates. It also records Japanese domestic enforcement proposals, new extraterritorial opium and narcotics ordinances for China and Manchukuo, and shipping-company searches prompted by U.S. fines. Correspondence, telegrams, cross-reference sheets, League of Nations material, and press clippings reveal persistent U.S. concern about weak penalties, official indifference to exports, corruption, and Japanese reactions to international criticism.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of despatch No. 533 on narcotics smuggling at Kobe and Osaka
subfiles.from: Kenneth C. Krentz, American Consul at Kobe
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese supervision of narcotics traffic through Kobe and Osaka and official attitudes toward drug exports.
subfiles.summary: Krentz concludes Kobe and Osaka authorities can know of narcotics movements but show little interest in exports; possible junior-official bribery, a procurator bribery case, and light export sentences.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 136: Narcotics Smuggling at the Port of Yokohama
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.about: Describes numerous opportunities for smuggling narcotics into and out of Yokohama Harbor.
subfiles.summary: Boyce reports weak searches of ships, launches, cargo, crews, visitors, and transshipments at Yokohama. He emphasizes the access and coercive power of organized peddlers, apparent police connivance, compromised watchmen, and the inability of private shipping precautions to provide effective control.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to instruction on the Taiyo Maru cocaine seizure
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to an instruction concerning cocaine seized aboard the S.S. Taiyo Maru at San Francisco.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: instruction on the October 10 San Francisco Taiyo Maru cocaine seizure, to be raised with the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Tokyo telegram concerning Hajime Hoshi
subfiles.about: Transmits a Tokyo telegram about a temporary visitor’s visa issued to suspected trafficker Hajime Hoshi.
subfiles.summary: State sends the Narcotics Commissioner the November 4 Tokyo telegram on Hoshi, suspected of complicity in illicit narcotics traffic.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Kobe and Yokohama port-smuggling reports
subfiles.about: Forwards consular reports about controls on access to ships at Kobe and Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: State sends Kobe Despatch No. 533 and Yokohama Despatch No. 136 on measures to prevent narcotics smuggling into and out of Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 149 requesting Inagaki’s status
subfiles.about: Requests the full name, title, and official status of the Japanese consular employee Inagaki.
subfiles.summary: Telegram asks who Inagaki is and his position at the Japanese Consulate in Geneva, reportedly handling part of Kusama's narcotics work.

subfiles.title: Progress-report extract on Japan’s Geneva narcotics contact
subfiles.about: Identifies Inagaki as the new Geneva contact for illicit-traffic cases involving Japanese subjects.
subfiles.summary: Progress report: Kusama's appointment to the Permanent Central Opium Board required a new contact; Inagaki at Geneva was designated for illicit narcotics cases involving Japanese subjects.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 678 describing Morikatsu Inagaki’s position
subfiles.about: Reports Morikatsu Inagaki’s unofficial title and duties at the Japanese Consulate in Geneva.
subfiles.summary: Inagaki is a non-career employee of two years without title, who took over most of Kusama's work; Yokoyama remains the Opium Advisory Committee representative.

subfiles.title: Continuation of narcotics-information exchange through Inagaki
subfiles.about: Approves continuing the informal exchange of narcotics-seizure information with Inagaki.
subfiles.summary: The note reviews the arrangement for supplying Japanese representatives with police information about U.S. seizures involving Japanese persons or suspected Japanese drugs. In light of the Geneva consul’s explanation of Inagaki’s role, the Department perceives no objection to continuing the arrangement through him.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo concerning Inagaki and the Geneva arrangement
subfiles.about: Informs the Embassy of Inagaki’s role and the Department’s decision to continue informal narcotics cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Instruction to Tokyo: Morikatsu Inagaki has taken over Kusama's Geneva work, and Treasury will be told the seizure-information exchange may continue with him.

subfiles.title: Japanese Government annual report on opium and dangerous drugs for 1934
subfiles.about: Introduces Japan’s annual report on opium and other dangerous drugs for 1934.
subfiles.summary: Cover of Japan's 1934 annual opium and dangerous drugs report, covering Japan proper, Korea, Taiwan, Kwantung, the South Seas and Hankow and Tientsin concessions.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japan’s 1934 drug report to the Public Health Service
subfiles.about: Forwards Japan’s annual opium and dangerous-drugs report for use by the U.S. Public Health Service.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Japan's 1934 drug report (League document O.C./A.R.1934/58) to the Public Health Service, submitted under the 1931 Convention.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japan’s 1934 drug report to the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.to: The Secretary of the Treasury, Bureau of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Sends the Japanese annual drug report to the Commissioner of Narcotics.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Japan's 1934 drug report to the Commissioner of Narcotics, citing the 1931 Convention and League document number.

subfiles.title: Treasury acknowledgment of the Japanese annual report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Japan’s 1934 annual report for the Public Health Service.
subfiles.summary: Treasury acknowledges receipt of State's March 20 communication on Japan's annual drug report.

subfiles.title: Telegram announcing Harriss’s arrival at Seattle
subfiles.about: Reports the expected Seattle arrival of informant James Lionel Harriss aboard the Heian Maru.
subfiles.summary: Telegram refers to Despatch No. 221 on Max Schwartz's suspected narcotics activities and says Harriss, the source of the allegations, is traveling to Seattle.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 221: Suspected Narcotic Smuggling Activities of Max Schwartz
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports Harriss’s allegations that Max Schwartz was arranging narcotics shipments to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Harriss said William Lewis had carried a Schwartz package aboard the Chichibu Maru but threw it overboard before reaching San Francisco. He also described Schwartz’s communications with Richard Soriano in Shanghai and alleged plans to use Schwartz’s teenage daughter as a future courier.

subfiles.title: Consulate General memorandum on Max Schwartz’s photographic enterprise
subfiles.about: Provides background on Schwartz’s efforts to establish a photographic business through a Japanese nominal owner.
subfiles.summary: Schwartz sought advice after Japan refused him a business license and proposed using a Japanese license-holder; the Consulate warned that the deception could bring serious trouble with the gendarmerie.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the Schwartz despatch and Harriss travel telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards the Max Schwartz report and notice of Harriss’s impending arrival at Seattle.
subfiles.summary: State sends Despatch No. 221 and the June 26 telegram on Harriss, an incoming Heian Maru passenger, to the Acting Narcotics Commissioner.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1913: Control of Narcotic Drugs in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports plans by the Japanese Home Office to tighten domestic narcotics controls.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses a press article and a conversation memorandum indicating stricter policing of traffickers, addicts, physicians, and druggists. He suggests that League criticism and an incident at Otsu involving Prince Kan'in Kotohito may have prompted the policy change.

subfiles.title: Home Office Seeks Narcotics Control
subfiles.from: The Japan Advertiser, reporting the Asahi Shimbun
subfiles.about: Reports an increase in Japanese narcotics addiction and planned police action against illegal prescribing and trafficking.
subfiles.summary: Home Office says registered addiction figures understate the problem, partly from unnecessary prescriptions; Kameyama announces strict inspection of doctors and druggists.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Shigeru Kuriyama on narcotics legislation
subfiles.about: Records Kuriyama’s explanation of planned stronger narcotics laws and the Hyogo smuggling investigation.
subfiles.summary: Kuriyama says the Home Office will initially use existing laws but is preparing legislation with heavier penalties, possibly including fuller implementation of the 1931 Convention. He adds that many of the twenty-six people arrested in Hyogo entered narcotics trafficking to finance gambling.

subfiles.title: Transmission of despatch No. 1913 on Japanese narcotics control
subfiles.about: Forwards Grew’s report and enclosures on Japan’s proposed stricter narcotics controls.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Despatch No. 1913 on Japanese narcotics control with a press clipping and Embassy conversation memorandum.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 161 identifying Tsuneji Arai
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports that arrested seamen named Tsuneji Arai of Seattle as their U.S. narcotics receiver.
subfiles.summary: Telegram: newspapers said nine seamen arrested at Kobe were examined on narcotics smuggling to the US; Tsuneji Arai described as an important trafficker, address unknown.

subfiles.title: Treasury notification concerning Tsuneji Arai
subfiles.about: Relays the Embassy telegram naming Tsuneji Arai as a narcotics receiver.
subfiles.summary: Treasury told that Tsuneji Arai, reportedly of Seattle, was implicated by nine seamen arrested at Kobe.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting further information on Arai
subfiles.about: Orders the Embassy to investigate the Kobe seamen and establish Arai’s identity.
subfiles.summary: Telegram asks the Embassy for further identifying information on Arai.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmission of the Harriss interview records
subfiles.about: Transmits Customs documents recording Harriss’s Seattle interview about Max Schwartz.
subfiles.summary: Treasury sends the Customs letter and reports on Harriss's allegations about Schwartz.

subfiles.title: Bureau of Customs letter forwarding Seattle reports
subfiles.from: Edson J. Shamhert, Bureau of Customs Division of Enforcement
subfiles.about: Forwards the supervising agent’s reply and Inspector Polite’s interview memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Bureau of Customs says Harriss's case went to its Seattle supervising agent and asks that Polite's memorandum be returned.

subfiles.title: Seattle Customs report on the Harriss interview
subfiles.from: Joseph L. Green, Supervising Customs Agent
subfiles.about: Reports compliance with instructions to interview Harriss and recommends surveillance of Schwartz.
subfiles.summary: Green encloses Inspector Polite's interview with Harriss; since Schwartz remained in Yokohama, foreign representatives should watch him.

subfiles.title: Inspector Polite’s memorandum of interview with James Lionel Harriss
subfiles.about: Records Harriss’s detailed account of Schwartz, Lewis, Soriano, and an alleged narcotics-smuggling venture.
subfiles.summary: Harriss describes joining Schwartz's photography business and growing suspicious in Yokohama; he says Lewis admitted carrying narcotics through Soriano, throwing them overboard and expecting to share proceeds with Schwartz.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Harriss interview to Yokohama
subfiles.about: Sends Customs records of Harriss’s Seattle examination for use in the Schwartz investigation.
subfiles.summary: Instruction forwards Treasury's Harriss material to Yokohama, with a copy to Shanghai for the Treasury representative.

subfiles.title: Instruction forwarding the Harriss interview to Shanghai
subfiles.about: Sends Customs interview records to Shanghai in connection with the Schwartz case.
subfiles.summary: Instruction sends Shanghai copies of Treasury's letter on Schwartz and its enclosures for the Consulate General and Treasury representative.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1950: Foreign Office Ordinances for Japanese Narcotics Traffickers in China and Manchuria
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains three new Japanese extraterritorial ordinances governing opium and narcotics in China and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Grew reports that the ordinances apply to Japanese nationals under consular jurisdiction and retain maximum penalties of only three months’ imprisonment or one hundred yen. He explains the separation of opium from manufactured-drug rules and the need for a special Manchukuo ordinance after Japan partially relinquished extraterritoriality there.

subfiles.title: Foreign Office Ordinance No. 10: Control of Opium in China
subfiles.from: Hachiro Arita, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Japanese subjects under consular jurisdiction in China
subfiles.about: Prohibits poppy cultivation and most dealings in raw or prepared opium in China.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance bans cultivation, import, export, manufacture, sale, purchase, possession, transfer, and transportation of specified opium products and smoking utensils. Violations, attempts, and assistance to non-Japanese offenders carry up to three months’ penal servitude or a one-hundred-yen fine, and the measure replaces the 1928 ordinance on July 1, 1936.

subfiles.title: Foreign Office Ordinance No. 11: Control of Narcotics in China
subfiles.from: Hachiro Arita, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Japanese subjects under consular jurisdiction in China
subfiles.about: Establishes licensing, recordkeeping, storage, inspection, and penalty rules for manufactured narcotics in China.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance defines narcotics broadly, prohibits manufacture, export, nonmedical use, and unauthorized transactions, and permits tightly controlled medical or scientific importation. It regulates prescriptions, sales, unused or spoiled stocks, storage, annual records, consular inspections, confiscation, and responsibility for employees, with maximum imprisonment of three months or a one-hundred-yen fine.

subfiles.title: Foreign Office Ordinance No. 12: Control of Narcotics in Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Hachiro Arita, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.to: Japanese subjects under consular jurisdiction in Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Imposes narcotics controls on Japanese subjects in Manchukuo outside the South Manchuria Railway Zone.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance closely parallels the China rules by defining controlled substances and regulating importation, professional use, prescriptions, transfers, storage, accounts, inspection, and confiscation. It takes effect on July 1, 1936, but expressly excludes the South Manchuria Railway Zone and retains the same limited penalties.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese newspaper clippings on narcotics criticism
subfiles.about: Forwards photostats of Osaka Mainichi and Japan Chronicle articles about international narcotics criticism.
subfiles.summary: Transmits English-language Japanese press pieces debating accusations that Japan tolerated or encouraged drug trafficking.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Antenna: response to accusations against Japan
subfiles.from: E. M., Osaka Mainichi English Edition
subfiles.about: Defends Japan against Stuart Fuller’s accusation of tolerance toward international narcotics trafficking.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo Antenna column concedes many Japanese join illicit drug trade but denies Japan encourages it, blaming demand, geography and trade.

subfiles.title: Japan Chronicle editorial criticizing the Mainichi’s narcotics argument
subfiles.about: Criticizes contradictions in the Osaka Mainichi’s defense of Japanese narcotics policy.
subfiles.summary: Japan Chronicle editorial criticizes the Mainichi's claims that Japan does its best and cannot control smugglers, questioning why tolerating the China drug trade would be national suicide.

subfiles.title: State Department analysis and transmission of the China and Manchukuo ordinances
subfiles.about: Forwards despatch No. 1950 while assessing the new ordinances’ scope and practical weakness.
subfiles.summary: State analyzes China and Manchukuo ordinances: they cover Koreans and make little difference south of the Great Wall; Ordinance No. 12's three-month or one-hundred-yen penalties are inadequate.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1988: Nippon Yusen Kaisha narcotics searches
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a new organized system for searching Nippon Yusen Kaisha vessels before departure for the United States.
subfiles.summary: The Osaka Mainichi attributed the searches to concern for Japan’s reputation and to heavy U.S. fines following repeated smuggling attempts by crewmen. Ship’s officers and seamen would conduct the searches, focusing on narcotics said to originate chiefly in Shanghai and Hong Kong, while seeking cooperation with Japanese and American authorities.

subfiles.title: Transmission of despatch No. 1988 on Nippon Yusen Kaisha
subfiles.about: Forwards the report on Nippon Yusen Kaisha’s new anti-smuggling searches.
subfiles.summary: Transmits Despatch No. 1988: Nippon Yusen Kaisha's action appears to follow strict fines for unmanifested opium and narcotics.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 248: Impending Departure of Max Schwartz and Ben Lessing
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.about: Warns that Schwartz and Lessing intend to sail from Yokohama to the United States.
subfiles.summary: Schwartz and Lessing displayed Nippon Yusen Kaisha ticket envelopes and said they planned to depart on September 27. Boyce identifies the scheduled ship as the Taiyo Maru, due at San Francisco on October 12, and proposes telegraphic confirmation if the travelers depart.

subfiles.title: Treasury notification of Schwartz and Lessing’s intended departure
subfiles.about: Forwards the Yokohama warning that Schwartz and Lessing may soon travel to the United States.
subfiles.summary: The note recounts their announced September 27 sailing and the Taiyo Maru’s expected October 12 arrival at San Francisco. Treasury is cautioned that they might use another vessel, while the Consulate promises to confirm their departure.

subfiles.title: Telegram confirming departure of Schwartz and Lessing
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul at Yokohama
subfiles.about: Confirms that Schwartz, his family, and Ben Lessing sailed aboard the Taiyo Maru.
subfiles.summary: Telegram: Schwartz, wife, two children and Lessing depart, due at Honolulu October 5 and San Francisco October 12.

subfiles.title: Treasury notification confirming the Taiyo Maru sailing
subfiles.about: Provides written confirmation that Schwartz and Lessing sailed for San Francisco aboard the Taiyo Maru.
subfiles.summary: Treasury confirms the Taiyo Maru sailing of suspected narcotics accomplices, enclosing the September 28 Yokohama telegram.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Beriah M. Thompson’s investigations
subfiles.about: Points to a report on Treasury agent Beriah M. Thompson’s investigations and conversations with Japanese officials.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 2049 on Beriah Thompson's investigations in Japan and dealings with Japanese officials.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to plan for another Treasury attaché at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram discussing Thompson’s proposal for a second Treasury attaché devoted solely to narcotics.
subfiles.summary: Dickover finds another Treasury attaché at Tokyo feasible but not a replacement for the information exchange; Japan seems receptive to suppression.
